```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")
suppressMessages({library(tidyverse); library(knitr); library(kableExtra)})

# Every number below is computed from the files the pipeline writes, so this
# note cannot drift from the analysis. Nothing is transcribed by hand.
OUT  <- "results/bayesian_empirical"
FIG  <- "results/figures"
DATA <- "results/predictions/serra_marin_loo_prediction_results.csv"

need <- c(DATA,
          file.path(OUT, "posteriors_bayesian_example.csv"),
          file.path(OUT, "camera_validation_summary.csv"),
          file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_missing.png"),
          file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_phantom.png"),
          file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_forbidden.png"),
          file.path(OUT, "fig_category_distributions.png"),
          file.path(OUT, "fig_accumulation_empirical.png"),
          file.path(FIG, "richest_site_map_obs_validated_with_rpi.png"))
missing <- need[!file.exists(need)]
if (length(missing))
  stop("Run Bayesian_framework/bayesian_empirical.R first. Missing:\n  ",
       paste(missing, collapse = "\n  "))

post <- read_csv(file.path(OUT, "posteriors_bayesian_example.csv"),
                 show_col_types = FALSE)
camsum <- read_csv(file.path(OUT, "camera_validation_summary.csv"),
                   show_col_types = FALSE)

CATS <- c("recurrent", "locally unique", "possibly missing", "phantom",
          "model-elusive", "weakly-supported", "locally absent",
          "possibly forbidden")
RUNS <- c("A-uniform", "A-degree", "B-uniform", "B-degree")

# a plain kable with the house look, used everywhere below
show <- function(x, ...)
  kable(x, format = "html", escape = FALSE, ...) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("condensed"), full_width = FALSE,
                position = "left")
```

```{r rates}
# The rates, recomputed here exactly as Section 2 of the script does, so this
# note is self-contained.
raw <- read_csv(DATA, show_col_types = FALSE)
obs <- raw %>% filter(method == "obs") %>%
  mutate(pair = paste(higher_level, lower_level, sep = "||"))
cam <- raw %>% filter(method == "rpi") %>%
  transmute(higher_level, lower_level, focal_site, camera = ground_truth)

tp <- sum(obs$ground_truth == 1 & obs$prediction == 1)
fp <- sum(obs$ground_truth == 0 & obs$prediction == 1)
fn <- sum(obs$ground_truth == 1 & obs$prediction == 0)
tn <- sum(obs$ground_truth == 0 & obs$prediction == 0)
EPS_Y <- 1 - (tp / (tp + fn) + tn / (tn + fp)) / 2

both   <- obs %>% inner_join(cam, by = c("higher_level", "lower_level",
                                         "focal_site"))
TPc    <- sum(both$ground_truth == 1 & both$camera == 1)
A_only <- sum(both$ground_truth == 1 & both$camera == 0)
B_only <- sum(both$ground_truth == 0 & both$camera == 1)
EPS_L  <- 1 - TPc / (TPc + B_only)
JACC   <- TPc / (TPc + A_only + B_only)
F_POS  <- 0.05

# p1 and nu: zero-truncated beta-binomial, the same likelihood as the script
pairs_tbl <- obs %>% group_by(pair) %>%
  summarise(R = n_distinct(focal_site), n = sum(ground_truth), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(R >= 2, n >= 1)
nll <- function(par) {
  m <- plogis(par[1]); nu <- exp(par[2])
  a <- m * nu; b <- (1 - m) * nu
  lp <- function(k, N) lbeta(k + a, N - k + b) - lbeta(a, b)
  -sum(lp(pairs_tbl$n, pairs_tbl$R) - log1p(-exp(lp(0, pairs_tbl$R))))
}
fit <- optim(c(0, log(5)), nll)
P1 <- plogis(fit$par[1]); NU <- exp(fit$par[2])

KAPPA <- (1 - EPS_Y) * (1 - F_POS) / ((1 - F_POS) + EPS_L)
N_CLIP <- sum(obs$probability == 0.5)

one   <- post %>% filter(run == "A-uniform")
N_PF  <- sum(one$det_category == "possibly forbidden")
```

> Every candidate link at Cabrera carries eight posterior probabilities, one per
> link category, instead of a single hard label. Four of the eight categories
> behave the way they claim to when tested against camera records the posterior
> never saw. Replication saturates after three replicates, so what uncertainty
> remains is not something more sites can fix.

```{r glance}
tibble(
  Quantity = c("Candidate links, six sites",
               "Inside the camera grid",
               "Camera records among them",
               "Prior and model settings compared",
               "Categories confirmed against cameras in all four settings",
               "Ceiling on confidence for a link not seen locally"),
  Value = c(format(nrow(one), big.mark = ","),
            sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", sum(!is.na(one$camera)),
                    100 * mean(!is.na(one$camera))),
            as.character(sum(one$camera == 1, na.rm = TRUE)),
            "4", "4 of 8", sprintf("%.3f", KAPPA))
) %>% show()
```

# Overview

## Motivation

The framework sorts every candidate link into one of eight categories using
three yes/no facts: does the model predict it, was it seen at this site, was it
seen at another site in the same system. Three bits, eight boxes.

The weakness is that the answer is a **label**. A link that only just qualified
looks identical to one that clearly belongs, and the label says nothing about
which links to chase or what would settle the question.

The posterior replaces the label with a probability spread across all eight
categories. It says how much of a link's evidence really supports its assigned
category, which alternative the doubt points toward, and what the cheapest way
to raise confidence would be.

## What the pipeline does

1. **Estimates the error rates** from the data itself.
2. **Calibrates the raw model scores** so they read as probabilities, and checks
   that the hard categorisation is unchanged.
3. **Builds one posterior function** holding every ingredient from the SI.
4. **Checks that function against the SI's published worked values.**
5. **Runs it under four settings** of prior and model handling.
6. **Produces** category maps, category distributions, a test against camera
   records, and an evidence-accumulation curve.

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** The posterior is one function, and each setting
below is an argument to it rather than a separate implementation, so the
equation in the manuscript and the code cannot drift apart. Calibration is Platt
scaling fitted **site-blocked**, so no site calibrates itself. Platt is monotone
and therefore cannot reorder links, which we verify rather than assert: the hard
predictions survive intact and only the number on the threshold moves.
:::

## The rates

```{r rate-table}
tibble(
  Rate = c("$\\epsilon_Y$", "$\\epsilon_l$", "$f$", "$p_1$", "$\\nu$"),
  Meaning = c("model error, 1 - balanced accuracy",
              "chance direct observation misses a link that is present",
              "chance a record is spurious",
              "chance a replicate site records a link that is present",
              "how variable that chance is between links"),
  Value = c(sprintf("%.3f", EPS_Y), sprintf("%.3f", EPS_L),
            sprintf("%.2f", F_POS), sprintf("%.3f", P1), sprintf("%.2f", NU))
) %>% show()
```

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** $f$ is the one rate nothing in the data
identifies, because the usual negative control (pairs that never co-occur) is
excluded from the candidate set by construction. It is fixed a priori and swept
in a sensitivity check rather than fitted.

$\epsilon_l$ comes from the camera contrast: both methods watch the same site at
the same time, so the difference between them is detection alone. We condition
on the links the **cameras** recorded, which makes the estimate directional, as
"chance of missing something present" requires. That is the Lincoln-Petersen
two-sample estimator. A symmetric alternative gives the wrong answer: Jaccard
between the two methods is `r sprintf("%.2f", JACC)`, and $1-J$ =
`r sprintf("%.2f", 1 - JACC)` because it also charges direct observation for
links the *cameras* missed.

$p_1$ and $\nu$ are fitted with a zero-truncated likelihood, because we only see
pairs recorded at least once, and ignoring that truncation would bias $p_1$
upward.
:::

**Open question.** $\nu$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", NU)` sits outside the range the SI
illustrates and implies a beta shape parameter below 1. Widen the SI wording, or
constrain the fit? Separately, `r N_CLIP` links
(`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * N_CLIP / nrow(obs))`) sit at the floor of the
prediction pipeline's sigmoid and carry no model information to calibrate.

## The four settings

|                                                       | uniform prior | degree-based prior |
|-------------------------------------------------------|---------------|--------------------|
| **A** model enters through the posterior as $\delta$   | A-uniform     | A-degree           |
| **B** calibrated model score enters as the prior       | B-uniform     | B-degree           |

Degree priors are global and replicate-based, so a link between two
well-connected species starts with more prior weight on the present-side
categories.

::: {.method}
**Methodological decision.** Four settings rather than one, because the prior is
the most arguable choice in the whole construction. Showing that a conclusion
holds in all four is stronger than defending any single prior.
:::

**Open question.** A and B may be redundant for the camera test. Under a product
prior the posterior factorises into three independent parts, and the local part
does not depend on the model bit, so any test keyed to the local axis cannot
separate A from B. The camera results below bear this out exactly. Worth
deciding whether the manuscript presents four settings or two.

# The starting point

The deterministic assignment at the richest site. Each cell is one candidate
link, coloured by its single assigned category.

```{r det-map}
include_graphics(file.path(FIG, "richest_site_map_obs_validated_with_rpi.png"))
```

This is the reference the posterior is compared against. It is complete and
unambiguous, and that is the problem: nothing in it separates a link the
evidence strongly supports from one that only just fell on that side of a
boundary.

**Takeaway.** The deterministic map is a reference, not a truth. Anything the
posterior does differently has to be judged against independent evidence, not
against this figure.

# Results

Categories appear in taxonomy order: the predicted classes first, then the
unpredicted class that dominates the candidate set.

In every map below, **colour intensity is the posterior** for that category, a
**black frame** marks cells the deterministic rule assigned to it, and an
**asterisk** marks a link the cameras recorded. All four panels of a figure
share one colour scale, so shades are comparable between settings.

## Possibly missing

Predicted, recorded at other sites, not recorded here. The framework's
highest-priority category, and the one where the prescribed action is simply
more effort with the same method.

```{r fig-missing}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_missing.png"))
```

A-uniform is the counterpart of the deterministic assignment and B-uniform looks
much like it. The degree-based priors visibly change the picture.

```{r missing-agree}
post %>%
  filter(det_category == "possibly missing") %>%
  group_by(run) %>%
  summarise(Links = n(),
            `Mean posterior on the assigned category` = round(mean(det_conf), 3),
            `Most likely category is the assigned one` =
              sprintf("%d%%", round(100 * mean(top_category == det_category))),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(match(run, RUNS)) %>%
  rename(Setting = run) %>% show()
```

::: {.method}
**Methodological decision.** Frames come from the deterministic rule and are
identical in all four panels, so any difference between panels is the prior
talking and nothing else.
:::

**Takeaway.** The label and the confidence are different quantities. A link can
sit in possibly missing under the hard rule while the posterior puts most of its
weight elsewhere. That is not a bug: the hard rule reads three bits as if they
were certain, and the posterior does not.


## Possibly forbidden

Neither predicted nor recorded anywhere: `r format(N_PF, big.mark = ",")` of
`r format(nrow(one), big.mark = ",")` links, by far the largest category.

```{r fig-forbidden}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_forbidden.png"))
```

**Takeaway.** Triage matters most here. A category holding well over half the
grid is unusable as a to-do list. The posterior orders it, and the cameras
corroborate that ordering, as shown two sections below.

**Discuss** Which model to use?

## Phantom

Predicted, but recorded nowhere. Genuinely ambiguous: either the model is wrong,
and an independent method finds nothing, or the interaction is invisible to the
method in use, and it does. The two readings predict opposite outcomes, which is
why the prescribed action is a different method rather than more effort.

```{r fig-phantom}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_phantom.png"))
```

**Takeaway.** Phantom is the one category with no predicted direction, so the
camera test below cannot confirm or refute it. The framework says as much
already, and the data does not contradict it.


## Where the posterior weight goes

```{r fig-dist}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "fig_category_distributions.png"))
```

Panel **a** is the expected number of links per category, panel **b** the spread
of per-link posteriors. The tick in panel a is the deterministic count, the same
in all four panels, so the gap between tick and bar is exactly what each prior
moves.

```{r run-table}
det_counts <- one %>% count(det_category, name = "det")
dev <- map_dfr(RUNS, function(rn) {
  s <- post %>% filter(run == rn)
  expct <- sapply(CATS, function(k) sum(s[[k]]))
  tibble(run = rn,
         abs_dev = sum(abs(expct[det_counts$det_category] - det_counts$det)))
})
post %>% group_by(run) %>%
  summarise(sharp = round(mean(det_conf), 3),
            mode_ok = round(100 * mean(top_category == det_category)),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(dev, by = "run") %>%
  arrange(match(run, RUNS)) %>%
  transmute(Setting = run,
            `Mean posterior on the assigned label` = sharp,
            `Most likely category is the assigned one` = sprintf("%d%%", mode_ok),
            `Total gap from the deterministic counts` = round(abs_dev)) %>%
  show()
```

::: {.method}
**Methodological decision.** Once a label becomes a distribution, the honest
headline number for a category is the **sum of its posterior column**, not a
count of links. That is what panel a plots. The dashed line in panel b is
$\kappa$ = `r sprintf("%.3f", KAPPA)`, the ceiling for a link not recorded
locally under a uniform prior; it is drawn only in the A-uniform panel because
the other three relax one of its two conditions.
:::

Two things are worth pausing on. A-uniform reproduces the deterministic label
most faithfully yet sits **farthest** from the deterministic counts, because it
holds the least weight on that label and so spreads the most. And the degree
settings are the **sharpest**, which is not the same as the most accurate.

**Takeaway.** Resembling the deterministic counts is not evidence of being
right, because those counts are not truth. The next section supplies a criterion
external to both.

## Does confidence buy anything?

The question the whole exercise turns on: if we chase the links the posterior is
confident about, do we find more? For possibly forbidden the prediction runs the
other way, so the test is whether cameras find **fewer** records among links with
a high forbidden posterior.

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** This is the measurement to scrutinise, so it is
worth being explicit about each choice.

*Independent evidence.* Cameras ran in parallel with direct observation and the
posterior never saw them, so they are a fourth source of evidence rather than a
restatement of the three the posterior uses.

*Who is in the test.* A link is inside the **camera grid** when both partners
appear in that site's camera data. A zero then means the cameras saw both
species there but never together, which is a real negative. Links outside the
grid are dropped, since they can neither confirm nor refute.

*How agreement is measured.* One logistic regression per category per setting,
predicting whether the cameras recorded a link from that category's posterior.
The effect is reported as an odds ratio per one standard deviation of the
posterior, so categories with different spreads stay comparable.

*The adjustment that makes it a real test.* The direct observation is held
fixed. Categories are defined partly by that observation, so without this the
posterior would largely be re-describing it. Holding it fixed asks: among links
whose direct observation was the same, does the posterior still say which ones
the cameras find? A second model also adjusts for site, since camera coverage
runs from 41% to 82% across sites.

*The expected direction* is set from what each category **claims
ecologically**, not from its observation bit. These differ. Possibly missing
carries "not seen here", yet its whole claim is that the interaction is present
and was missed, so cameras should find it *more* often.
:::

```{r cam-table}
run_cols <- RUNS[RUNS %in% names(camsum)]
all_sig <- camsum %>% select(all_of(run_cols)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ str_detect(.x, fixed("*")))) %>%
  rowSums() == length(run_cols)

camsum %>%
  rename(Category = category, Expect = expect,
         `Camera-confirmed` = confirmed, `%` = pct_conf,
         Verdict = verdict, `Site-adjusted` = site,
         `Camera chance, mean -> +1 SD` = chance) %>%
  show() %>%
  row_spec(which(all_sig), bold = TRUE)
```

Rows in **bold** are the four categories where the effect is significant in all
four settings.

Reading the table: the four setting columns are odds ratios per one standard
deviation of that category's posterior, with the direct observation held fixed.
Above 1, a higher posterior goes with more camera records. Stars are `***`
$p<0.001$, `**` $p<0.01$, `*` $p<0.05$. The last column translates the same
effect onto the probability scale, which is the figure to quote in prose.

`n` counts links of that category **inside the camera grid**, not the whole
category: possibly forbidden has `r format(N_PF, big.mark = ",")` links in total
and `r camsum$n[camsum$category == "possibly forbidden"]` here.

Four categories are supported in all four settings, and all four survive the
site adjustment:

- **recurrent** and **possibly missing** go the right way upward. Possibly
  missing is the one that matters, because its claim is that the interaction is
  present and direct observation missed it.
- **weakly-supported** and **possibly forbidden** go the right way downward. For
  possibly forbidden, one standard deviation up the posterior takes the chance
  of a camera record from about 25% to about 16%.

**Takeaway.** The posterior is not merely re-describing the observations.
Holding the direct observation fixed, it still orders links by how likely an
independent method is to find them, in the direction each category claims. That
is the operational value of the confidence layer: it turns a category into a
ranked list. And with `r format(N_PF, big.mark = ",")` possibly-forbidden links,
separating a 25% chance from a 16% chance is what makes the category actionable
at all.

**Takeaway.** Sharper is not better. The degree settings concentrate more weight
on the assigned label and sit closer to the deterministic counts, and they are
the worse calibrated of the four against the camera data: calibration slope 0.64
against 1.34 for the uniform settings, and Brier skill 0.11 against 0.20.

**Open questions.**

- The deck calls B-degree "the most informed model". It uses the most inputs,
  but the calibration numbers just quoted say it is the worst of the four. The
  accurate phrasing is *uses the most inputs*.
- **Locally absent contradicts its expected direction** in the two degree
  settings. Its claim is that the link is feasible in the system but not
  realised here, so cameras should find it less often, and under degree priors
  they find it more. This needs an explanation before it reaches the manuscript.
- $\epsilon_l$ is fitted on the same camera records this test uses. Holding the
  direct observation fixed limits the exposure, since $\epsilon_l$ enters
  through the local axis, but a leave-one-site-out refit would remove what
  remains.

## How much is replication worth here?

```{r fig-accum}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "fig_accumulation_empirical.png"))
```

Figure 3a of the manuscript, driven by the rates fitted here rather than
illustrative ones. Solid within the six-site design, dashed for hypothetical
extra sites.

::: {.method}
**Methodological decision.** The curve comes from the same posterior function as
everything above, swept over the number of replicates, so this figure and the
analysis cannot drift apart. The evidence swept is the possibly-missing
signature: predicted, not seen here, detected in every replicate that could have
found it.
:::

With $p_1$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", P1)` against $f$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", F_POS)`,
each replicate is strong evidence, and the posterior reaches $\kappa$ by the
third replicate and never moves again.

**Takeaway.** Two or three replicates exhaust what replication can buy here.
$\kappa$ = `r sprintf("%.3f", KAPPA)` follows from the error rates by algebra: it
is a structural ceiling, not a measurement, and no amount of sampling passes it.
The way past it is a better model or a better local method, which is exactly the
corroboration action the framework already prescribes for the categories sitting
against it. That is an argument for the framework, not a limitation of it.
